name: Paperwork and Permits to Verify Before Window Installation in Los Angeles County

mainEntity.name: What should Los Angeles County homeowners check on a window installer’s paperwork and permits before any work starts to avoid inspection failures or stop-work orders?
mainEntity.text: What should Los Angeles County homeowners check on a window installer’s paperwork and permits before any work starts to avoid inspection failures or stop-work orders?

acceptedAnswer.text: In Los Angeles County, window projects can stall or fail inspection if the paperwork is incomplete. Before work starts, verify the installer holds an active, appropriately classified contractor’s license and can show proof of both liability and workers’ compensation insurance. Ask for a written contract describing the exact number of windows, locations, brands, and whether any openings are being enlarged, reduced, or converted to different styles. Next, clarify which permits are required in your city. Simple like-for-like replacements may sometimes be over-the-counter, but changes that affect egress, structure, or exterior appearance typically need full permits and inspections. Get a copy or permit number in writing; do not rely on verbal assurances that a permit is “not needed.” Request the product data sheets and NFRC labels for your chosen windows to confirm they meet current Title 24 U-factor and SHGC requirements. If any windows are near floors, doors, stairways, or wet areas, confirm that tempered or safety glazing is specified. Also ask how many inspections are expected (rough opening, final, etc.) and who will be present. Having these details up front significantly reduces the risk of stop-work orders, rework, or surprise costs when the inspector visits.
acceptedAnswer.description: Before window work starts in Los Angeles County, homeowners should confirm the contractor’s active license, required permits for structural or egress changes, city-specific inspection requirements, written scope of work tied to code compliance, proof of insurance, and manufacturer specs showing the selected windows meet Title 24 and safety glazing rules.
